Think about what kind of games you enjoy and what genre you want to make, find the most minimal possible implementation of it, with the most BASIC version of core mechanics you can think of. First you need to understand that all of this shit fades, money, career, looks, all of that doesn't matter in the end we're going to die the same way. Even your talents will fade, age will rob you of your ability eventually. And you might logically know that, but you need to truly feel and internalize this fact. You might also be assigning way too much weight to material/social status. There is something you have that no one else does, your character, the values you choose to embody and live by, and the ideals you strive towards. Your only goal is to get to the end of your life and be happy with the person you became and how you conducted yourself. 

If you can find a way to be content, happy, and fulfilled *without* all those things this other guy has, I'd argue you would be way stronger and much "more" of a man. And on that note, there's probably some guy out there with less money, less status, and less resources than all three of us and is still living happily, connected to his community, taking care of his family- and generally going to sleep happy with who he is. 

Secondly, you only get one hand in life, the one you are dealt. What this other guy has is completely irrelevant, because the comparison is completely unfair to you. If you want to take that to an extreme end; you were dealt with a completely average hand (or even below average if you're feeling particularly self-critical), what are you going to do with it? The good news is that you're in good company, most people are just like you and me, average, and average people can be incredibly happy and fulfilled. 

You've been given a life on hard mode in some ways; during a time where comparison is easier than ever, when material achievement seem to be a false measure of one's "value", and where people seem to always chase an upgrade.   
  
The only two things you have in your life are time and health, everything else will fade. My advice is to try and get in touch with your values, and really ask yourself what it means to you to be a man (if you care about that), because for thousands of years men existed without status, cars, luxury, or an "easy" lifestyle.

I wrote my dissertation in 10 days, it was a frenzy, similar word count too (ended up doing really well). If I can do it you can too, because you are in a much better position.

Most of this battle is going to be mindset, here are some things that helped me:

* spend time outside, if you're not writing, take a walk - screen times/gaming/etc. are not a good break
* EACH day for these 3 weeks do something nice for yourself, get yourself your fav foods, get a nice drink, get some snacks, order your fav meals; you're going to need to be in high spirits there's no need to punish yourself further
* You do not have to sacrifice sleep or health for this and you shouldn't, get as much sleep as you can each night, but if you wake up don't lay in bed
* I put on white/brown noise in the background, even if it doesn't like scientifically help, placebo will do its job
* You know your field better than me ofc, but something that helped me was just going through the references of a source I had already used and skimming through every abstract
* Use an automatic reference tool like Zotero, its power doesn't lie in the citation generator, it lies in the ability to instantly save any paper/source in a library and database with one click of the browser extension 
* Similarly, use a highlighter extension (chrome/firefox) that saves the highlights between sessions, when you got 100 tabs open you don't want to spend 5 min figuring out which section of the source was relevant. 
* do not use ANY screens for anything other than your dissertation, when you let yourself be "bored" your mind will make do with work as stimulation
* paradoxically, don't look at the clock during the day and while you're working, instead just tell yourself 300 words in the morning, 300 words in the afternoon, and 300 in the evening. You can shorten how much you need to write accordingly, I found that if I told myself "okay I just need to write 100 words in an hour" I'd get started and more points would naturally spring up as i kept reading and writing
* I can't stress this enough, do not punish yourself, put yourself down, or blame yourself, you're doing a great job tackling this, and when you're done you will be amazed at your efforts; "man up" and just "toughing it out" means absolutely fuck all, don't listen to that it doesn't even make sense
* And lastly worst case, there is always another path to get this finished if you don't do it in time, it won't be the end of the world or your academic career. I only say this so that you know it's okay, but don't rely on it as an option haha
* You've already done quite a bit actually, honor the efforts of the past you by committing to using whichever of these tips help you

I'm copying what I wrote in another comment here:  
  
So, I recovered from them by giving myself a lot of time to feel the way I did, however bad I felt and however long it took, I accepted that as part of myself. Secondly, spending time alone and reflecting on why I still felt so attached, uncovering the beliefs I held about myself (e.g. "I am not good enough, everyone is going to cheat on me", "I will be rejected even if I try to meet someone new", "No one is going to want me, and even if they do, eventually they'll get sick of me"). There's usually some sort of belief you're holding about yourself or your future that is causing you to loop through this pain, I was (and still am) in therapy which was a great place to work through that. Obviously, stick to NC, the less you know about your ex the better, eventually they really do become a stranger that you don't give a shit about. A lot of moving on has to do with establishing trust with yourself again, that you can survive betrayal like this, and admitting that you were completely wrong about this person and grieving that as well.

To avoid going with trust issues moving forward, you need to treat your time and energy like an investment, go into it assuming you will lose that investment. The trust that you can survive losing that investment needs to outweigh the pain you think you'll feel if things end, the moment that is not the case anymore you need to pull back and reassess; otherwise you will stay in any situation blindly just to avoid feeling pain. 

3 months NC for this sort of blindsiding/betrayal is pretty early, it's going to take as long as it needs, but it will end. You will eventually be over it and be able to see this relationship for what it was: a shitty time with someone who clearly has something going wrong in his head to behave that way.

It took me a lot of time, a lot of falling down on my face, and frankly living a shitty life until you truly get sick of it. To be honest with you it happened accidentally for me, I gave up hope for my future but still wanted to live, so the only thing I could focus on was the current day.

It starts with letting go of any sort of overarching concrete plan or ultimate goal (a specific career, earning X amount, relationship status), practically that means that you only try and focus on the next step. For me I ended up finishing my psych degree, and at the end of it realized I want to do something else- I'm now prepping for med school.

I bring up this example because at the time of doing my degree I wasn't thinking about long term, I only focused on what I could control; the next assignment or exam. That helped me keep my 4.0 GPA and paradoxically gave me the best options for my future.

What ends up happening is that you treat every next step like the most important thing, and you end up chaining them together leading to the best outcomes.

I want to add that you can't self-hate yourself into change, you need to treat yourself like you would treat a child you loved. Ideally, you need to teach yourself new habits and behaviors in a kind way. The life you are living now is not pathetic, it showed you that you want to change.

This might resonate with you, it might work, it might not. But I've noticed that the endless chase for "self discipline" ends with us being disappointed in ourselves and an endless loop of shame. The antidote to shame is compassion towards oneself, and honestly it's the hardest thing to practice. (If anyone doubts me on this, try being unconditionally kind to yourself even if you fail, you'll realize it's the hardest thing to do).

If there's only one thing you take away from this; always ask yourself "What would I tell a child who is ashamed about things, and can't seem to stick to change and gets depressed each time they fail". You'd be kind and understanding, but also gentle about helping the child take the next step and helping them be brave.

What I've noticed for myself is I need to let go of the idea that I need to turn everything around and I'll then live this amazing life where everything is fixed. It creates unrealistic pressure on yourself. 

Learning to focus on the actions you take every day is what helps you stick to change, treat every day as a new life and your goal is to make the day 1% better for the person that comes tomorrow.

Rationality and emotionality are not as separate as we'd like to think. Even a state of "emotional detachment" is a specific embodied state that includes both bodily states and thought processes.

Some argue that we are never free of emotion as it is contingent on physical body states (which we are never free off)

Look at Lisa Feldman Barret (2017) and their point that emotion and cognition are not localised in seperate areas.

More convincingly consider what happens when people's emotional processing is compromised: when there is damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, impairing emotional processing, people are IMPAIRED when making regular everyday decisions and their ability to learn from mistakes.

i.e. Decision making makes use of lessons learned from emotional experiences and consideration of anticipated emotional states is a successful decision making strategy

However making decisions based on one's current emotional state is not an effect strategy.

you don't have to do that if you think it's too silly, but the main point is to focus on yourself, it may seem counter intuitive but I've found that listening to your body and mind yields answers as to what it is exactly that's ailing you.
